name: Carbamazepine
summary: A sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant that is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia and a workhorse for focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures and bipolar mania.
mechanism: Use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing high-frequency neuronal firing; active epoxide metabolite contributes effect.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4) with autoinduction; active carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide metabolite

dosing.adult: Start 200 mg BID (IR) and titrate; usual maintenance 800–1200 mg/day

safety.pregnancy: Known teratogen — increased neural tube defects and major malformations; avoid when alternatives exist
contraindications: Known carbamazepine hypersensitivity (HLA-B*1502-associated SJS/TEN risk in Asian populations)
warnings: SJS/TEN — screen for HLA-B*1502 before starting in at-risk (Asian) patients
Aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis — monitor CBC
Potent CYP3A4 inducer with autoinduction — many drug interactions
monitoring: HLA-B*1502 screening in Asian patients before start
safety.overdose: Coma, respiratory depression, cardiac conduction disturbance (wide QRS); supportive care; activated charcoal and multidose charcoal enhance elimination

clinicalPearls: Autoinduction — levels fall over the first weeks of therapy; re-check levels after stabilization
Potent enzyme inducer — reduces efficacy of oral contraceptives, warfarin, and many other AEDs
good: Trigeminal neuralgia — still the first-line standard — and focal seizures when an enzyme inducer is acceptable.
bad: Patients on OCPs or warfarin, Asian patients untested for HLA-B*1502, or anyone at risk of hyponatremia.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard neurology/pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
